about: The vocabulary of reasons for choosing a play, built from the player's own words during play. Claude tags each explained play with these codes (catalog/annotations.jsonl). A new code starts as 'proposed' and becomes 'adopted' only when the player agrees; its definition uses the player's words.

reasons.name: Uncover the most hidden
reasons.definition: My normal goal is to uncover face-down cards on the column with the most face-down cards. The overarching strategy is to uncover the card on the columns that has the most potential to reveal more cards to be played. Tie-break: when two cards are available to play with the same number of face-down cards above them, playing either gives the same prospect, so I select the column that has been "least productive" relative to its initial potential productivity (the face-down cards it started with). This simplifies to "the playable card on the left-most column with the same (highest) number of face-down cards at the moment both cards simultaneously became playable." Late in the game, a column still holding many face-down cards (e.g. 5 on g) becomes worrisome, and uncovering it can outweigh the regular prescribed play (e.g. 4♥h over 3♠g, against home_pace): the "anecdotal" evidence is that most games I've lost seem to have the most unplayed face-down cards. At that stage it is partly gut feel.

reasons.name: Right-most playable first
reasons.definition: At the beginning of the game, I do this by selecting the right-most card that is playable.

reasons.name: Automatic home play
reasons.definition: An ace always goes straight to home since not playing it has the most downside (covering a face-down card, blocking a column from accepting a high card, preventing the next card in the home pile from being played, etc.). Moving an ace to home has only upside consequences. When more than one ace can go home, both aces will be played before any other play, so the order in which they're played is of no material consequence. When the ace of a suit is on the foundation and the two becomes playable, it is an automatic play because there is absolutely no progressive play value to leaving it unplayed. Likewise, since 2♥ and AT LEAST 2♦ have been played to home, playing 3♠ to home (on 2♠) is automatic: there is no progressive-play reason not to play it.

reasons.name: Keep options open
reasons.definition: I don't want to make that decision prematurely. Not playing either of them until I have a king to put in the columns is an unnecessary decision that locks me into a position before I know what's coming next. Leaving them in place leaves my options open. Emptying a column is worth it only with a king available to replace the card AND a queen of opposite color in the tableau that could play on the king AND lead to a new play OR reveal a face-down card in the tableau.

reasons.name: Only new plays
reasons.definition: A play is new only when it is "freshly available": the card to be played, or the card it would be played on, became available as a result of the most recent play; or the card to be played was just turned up on the waste by a stock turn (available "again", even if it was passed over on an earlier stock turn). A play is identified by its cards, not its columns: if the 8♦ moves to another column but stays continuously available, 7♣ onto the 8♦ is the same play and is not new again (unless the 8♦ is covered, or goes to the foundation and back, and becomes available again). For a king, the target is the empty column itself: a king-to-column play is new when the column has just been emptied or the king has just become available. After an Undo, the plays that were new when that position was first reached are new again. "NNP" (no new play): no new play, so I'll draw. "ONP" (only new play): multiple plays may be available, but the play I made was the only new play. A run moved from one card to a matching card is only a "useful" play when freeing up the card that the moved card is blocking becomes immediately playable.

reasons.name: Build the longer run
reasons.definition: When there is nothing else to consider, I play the 9 with the most run-cards on it. There may be no advantage in doing so, but I opt for continuing to build an existing longer run over starting or adding to a smaller one (all other things being equal).

reasons.name: King to an empty column
reasons.definition: Because my goal is to not use memory/card-counting, playing a king is an automatic play, similar to the reason for always playing an ace on its home pile. Exception: when the king would only serve as a place to play a queen that is already at the top of a column (e.g. K♠ for Q♦, already at the top of d), moving it to the empty column is "a wasted move".

history.name: King to an empty column

reasons.name: Seen this pass
reasons.definition: A card's progressive play value, judged by what I've seen in the current turn of the waste pile: e.g. playing 6♥ revealed 6♦, which I mentally note as potentially of no new progressive play value since I've not seen a black 5 in the current turn of the waste pile.

reasons.name: Keep a target
reasons.definition: Hold a card back from home when it can take a card I may want to play later: if the 3♣ becomes playable, it can be played on the 4♦. At this point in the game, the potential for a future play of 3♣ outweighs the relatively benign current move of 4♦ to home.

reasons.name: Home pace by colour
reasons.definition: As a general rule, I try not to play a card to home if it is more than two ranks higher than the lowest card of the opposite color currently played to a home pile. A suit whose ace hasn't been played counts as 0 (e.g. 0♣). It's an informal weighing of the odds: when not playing the card home gives no material advantage either, choosing WHERE to play it becomes the next consideration (e.g. 3♠h, since 3♠c would clog the 4♥ and duplicate the 3♣ as a target). When a pile is already further ahead than I prefer (e.g. 8♦ three ranks above 5♣, likely a strategic decision that went against the preference), adding to it (9♦h) "only compounds an already unpreferred situation."

reasons.name: Left-most target
reasons.definition: I consider both plays as essentially neutral unless there is a clear reason to leave one or the other open. As such, by default, a card with multiple targets is played on the left-most target card.

reasons.name: Hoping for a card
reasons.definition: In my mind, I'm hoping to reveal a particular card soon so a play can follow: e.g. a black 4 so I can reveal a card on g, especially because the stock pile is dwindling.

reasons.name: Offset the waste
reasons.definition: On the first draw of a new game I will almost always leave one card on the waste pile. This ensures that a subsequent turn of the stock pile will offset each card by two positions, which increases the likelihood of a playable card being turned up in the waste the next time through. (From my experience with draw-3 game play, regardless of how many plays can be made from the initial draw of a new game, the likelihood that subsequent draws from the stock will not expose any new plays seems to occur more often than one might intuit.) By using the offset method, I at least give myself a chance at having a progressive play after the next stock turn. As a general rule, this applies to each new pass too: whenever the last card in the waste pile is the only available play. The rule is enforced less and less as the stock is depleted (and "known" cards become more obvious); at some point it becomes a "gut feel" decision (perhaps informed later by how many stock turns remain). The size of the stock informs it: with more than three cards in the stock pile (the game shows when 3 or fewer remain, which I could easily know with a physical deck), I may decline to play the last waste card (e.g. 5♦, anywhere) and set up another play instead.

reasons.name: Tableau and home first
reasons.definition: I try to always maximize tableau and home plays before considering waste plays. tableau_first describes the plays from a tableau column to a tableau column, or from a tableau column to a home pile, made to exhaust as many tableau plays as possible before turning the stock. A waste play that was waiting while the tableau plays were made is not tableau_first: it is pending_waste.

A waste play made once the tableau plays are exhausted is not tableau_first: it is the only new play available after all tableau play (ONP).

reasons.name: Automatic plays first
reasons.definition: When plays are functionally equivalent, I find that making the automatic plays as soon as they're available helps me to see the next potential waste-card play more directly, reducing my likelihood of not seeing a "better" subsequent play than the one currently being considered.

reasons.name: Don't clog
reasons.definition: As long as I have a higher-rank card to play that will open a column for a king (e.g. 7♣c), I won't "clog" a card (the 4♦) with low cards (3♣ and 2♦). I would put that move off as much as possible, hoping for the A♣ and 2♣ to get played first.

reasons.name: Keep it moving
reasons.definition: A play made to keep the game "moving" (not necessarily progressing), e.g. the 3♥h-4♥h sequence.

reasons.name: Kings out
reasons.definition: An overarching principle: get all of the kings out as soon as possible. It seems intuitively progressive, affording the most flexibility and play availability, since it allows more options with the middle cards of a run (played down-rank on kings), and leads to more potential for cards in the remaining (unopen) columns to be revealed, and therefore played.

reasons.name: Foundation set
reasons.definition: An overarching principle: get all of the aces on the foundation as soon as possible. It seems intuitively progressive, affording the most flexibility and play availability, since it allows more options with the middle cards of a run (played up-rank on the foundation), and leads to more potential for cards in the remaining (unopen) columns to be revealed, and therefore played.

reasons.name: Gut feel
reasons.definition: A "gut feel" decision: intuitive hope/foresight or speculation, usually small and less impactful, that I can't easily define, because I don't have "perfect knowledge" of the stock pile and have zero knowledge of face-down tableau cards. Some decisions may ultimately have to remain as gut feel, but one of my goals is to minimize those with more informed rules that can still be derived without memorization tricks or card-counting hacks.

reasons.name: Cover the higher card
reasons.definition: Higher-rank cards won't be played to the foundation before lower-rank cards (unless I'm eventually forced into "keep moving" play at some point), so when I must cover a card, covering the higher one makes more sense: e.g. covering the 8♦ with the 7♣ rather than covering the 3♣ with the 2♦.

reasons.name: Don't duplicate a target
reasons.definition: Playing a card that would only duplicate an existing target's availability has no apparent clear material advantage: e.g. the 3♣ is available to take the 2♦ (and clear column d if another king becomes playable), so playing 3♠c would currently duplicate that availability.

reasons.name: Dead end
reasons.definition: No pending progressive plays on the tableau or to/from the foundation, and a new full stock turn completed with no new plays becoming available: I select End game. I only play to win: a play that doesn't progress game play (e.g. J♦g, with every card face up) isn't worth making when no other progressive plays are available. Playing out all the remaining available plays would only take extra plays to lose the game, which makes no sense.

history.name: Dead end
history.definition: No pending progressive plays on the tableau or to/from the foundation, and a new full stock turn completed with no new plays becoming available: I select End game.

reasons.name: Setup play
reasons.definition: A play that isn't a new play itself, but a setup for a more potentially advantageous play to follow: e.g. 7♠b opens column a for the K♠, moving toward Kings out! and unlocking the potential of five hidden cards. The play being set up may come more than one play after the setup play: don't expect it to happen immediately afterwards.

reasons.name: Pending waste play
reasons.definition: A play that was available on the waste pile, but pending until the tableau_first plays were exhausted; then it is made. It isn't a new play: it was waiting. E.g. 2♦b, available since the 3♠ became its target, played once the tableau plays were done.

reasons.name: Known play in the hole
reasons.definition: A play I hold in reserve (e.g. 4♥h), as long as play is moving, like having a "known play" in the hole to use when no other more advantageous plays are available. At some point it gets into gut-feel territory. In some ways it's the inverse of tableau_first, but less well defined. To remind myself that I have a play in the hole that will open a column to accept a king (e.g. 5♥g emptying f), I keep a mental note of it by saying to myself "Red 5." If a red 5 becomes playable from another column or the waste pile, I don't automatically play it: I reevaluate the game state to be sure playing it offers a clear advantage over hedging to keep the play for a king available.

history.name: Known play in the hole
history.definition: A play I hold in reserve (e.g. 4♥h), as long as play is moving, like having a "known play" in the hole to use when no other more advantageous plays are available. At some point it gets into gut-feel territory. In some ways it's the inverse of tableau_first, but less well defined.

reasons.name: Hedge play
reasons.definition: The more advantageous play that also hedges against an unfortunate card sequence: e.g. playing 9♠h to preserve the waste_offset in case of an unfortunate sequence in the last three waste cards, given the high potential to win based on the current game state.

reasons.name: Higher-rank first
reasons.definition: Prefer the more advantageous progressive play that moves higher-rank cards: it also has the potential to free up lower-rank cards and takes advantage of the "Kings out!" and "Foundation set" theory of upward and downward card play (e.g. waiting a few moves to play X♥ rather than 5♥h, 6♥h and 6♦g now).

reasons.name: Complex plays first
reasons.definition: When multiple plays are available, as long as not making one of the plays has no immediate detrimental effects if it remains unplayed, it's okay to leave it unplayed as long as not playing it is a "neutral" decision. I can't make two plays simultaneously, and I often focus on the more "complex" moves first: e.g. 4♥f to offset the waste pile before I forgot, while 3♠h waited a move.
